themes.name: Circadian Rest-Activity Rhythms (CRARs)
themes.description: This theme encompasses the definition, measurement, and specific metrics used to characterize circadian rest-activity rhythms (CRARs) in the context of human research.

themes.name: Main Effects of CRARs on Cognition
themes.description: This theme covers the direct associations found between circadian rest-activity rhythms and cognitive performance or decline, not considering moderating factors.

themes.name: Age-Dependent Cognitive Associations
themes.description: This theme details how the relationship between CRARs and cognitive performance or decline changes based on the age of the participants, highlighting specific age-related interactions.

themes.name: Sex/Gender-Dependent Cognitive Associations
themes.description: This theme explores how the relationship between CRARs and various cognitive domains (performance or decline) is moderated by an individual's sex or gender.

themes.name: Race-Dependent Cognitive Associations
themes.description: This theme focuses on claims demonstrating how the associations between CRARs and cognitive functions (performance or change over time) vary across different racial groups.

themes.name: APOE e4-Dependent Cognitive Associations
themes.description: This theme includes claims about how the relationship between CRARs and cognitive outcomes is moderated by the presence or absence of the APOE e4 allele.

themes.name: Study Design and Methodology
themes.description: This theme details the research design, participant selection, data collection methods (actigraphy, cognitive assessments), and the statistical approaches used in the study.

themes.name: Study Limitations
themes.description: This theme addresses the identified weaknesses and constraints of the research, including potential biases and methodological shortcomings that may affect the generalizability or interpretation of the findings.

themes.name: Future Research and Implications
themes.description: This theme outlines the suggestions for future studies, potential interventional strategies, and the broader significance of the current findings for cognitive health research.

claims.text: A growing body of literature highlights how a physically active lifestyle is associated with reduced risk of dementia, better cognitive functioning, physiological changes in the brain and overall wellbeing.
claims.deep: This Research Topic (RT) focused on the effects of physical activity (PA) on brain and cognitive functions across the lifespan. A growing body of literature highlights how a physically active lifestyle is associated with reduced risk of dementia, better cognitive functioning, physiological changes in the brain and overall wellbeing. In this vein, studies on people with a sedentary lifestyle highlight an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases and a higher rate of early mortality. However, many studies found contrasting or inconclusive results, depending on different targeted population, tests, and methodologies. Age and activity type seem to influence brain state, but underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This RT addresses how the brain and cognitive functioning is influenced by PA, as well as the psychological benefits of an active lifestyle across the lifespan. It contains 9 contributions on the effect of physical exercise on brain plasticity and cognitive functioning, including original research articles (5), systematic reviews and meta-analyses (3), and a brief research report (1). How can older adults counteract age-related declines and lead longer, healthier, and fuller working lives? Across the lifespan, the brain exhibits notable plasticity and adapts to environmental changes via modifying brain function and neural connectivity (Goh and Park, 2009; Park and Reuter-Lorenz, 2009; Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014). PA, cognitive training, and social engagement are major intervention approaches to improve brain health and cognitive functioning across the lifespan (Hillman et al., 2014; Ballesteros et al., 2015; Donnelly et al., 2016; Kramer and Colcombe, 2018; Ballesteros, 2022). A great deal of research supports that PA protects against age-related cognitive declines enhancing executive functions and memory (Hötting and Röder, 2013; Voelcker- Rehage and Niemann, 2013). This RT aims to provide a current picture of the state of the art on the effect of PA interventions on brain and cognition across the lifespan in healthy individuals and patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
claims.summary: A physically active lifestyle is linked to reduced dementia risk, improved cognitive function, brain physiological changes, and overall wellbeing.
